catalog_quote: [Gerfen 1999 ch. 3 abstract] both predictable and contrastive glottalization are licensed only under stress ... In §3.5, I provide an explicit characterization of the stress system ... [note 2] This choice reflects an analysis in which glottalization is limited to the first (stressed) mora of a couplet (see §3.4 below). ... [note 47] I do not consider stressless candidates under the assumption of an inviolable constraint in the grammar requiring that all words be stressed. ... [note 48] resulting in the construction of a single foot, exactly the CM case. ... [note 51] Note also that Parse-Mora is equally important for ruling out hypothetically unfooted candidates such as ’kunú kwii in which stress is incorrectly located on the first mora of the initial couplet ... [note 52] an alternative analysis exists in which stress can be viewed as obligatorily non-final in both the prosodic word and the root (NonFin(PrWd) » NonFin(Root)). ... These four ordered constraints would also appear to locate stress predictably on the penultimate mora of the final couplet of a prosodic word. ... [note 57] Also, as the subject NP and independent prosodic word, guru receives its own main stress. ... [Gerfen & Denisowski 1999 preprint p. 2] All were controlled for stress: (C)CVV couplets are stressed, and in (C)CVCV couplets, stress falls predictably on the first vowel.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (14 pp., text, Word/Acrobat 2001, header 'In Texas linguistic forum 41.. 57-69'). Preprint p. 2, §2 'Data Collection, Experimental Set-up, and Measurement' reads exactly: 'All were controlled for stress: (C)CVV couplets are stressed, and in (C)CVCV couplets, stress falls predictably on the first vowel.' Verbatim match. The other locators also check: p. 7 fn. 2 (continued on p. 8) 'two unstressed vowels which are themselves much shorter than their stressed V1 counterparts'; p. 10 'V1 of (C)CVCV couplets, i.e. on stressed vowels implementing a lexically specified tone target'. No other stress passages in the file (a full-text search for stress/accent per page). Identity: p. 1 'Coatzosp…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the first vowel (first mora) of the couplet, the bimoraic root that is the canonical lexical word: in CVCV couplets on V1, i.e. the penultimate (root-initial) syllable; in CVV couplets the single (long or diphthongal) syllable carries it. Stress is predictable, not lexical. Second-hand (Penner 2019 reporting Gerfen 1996:131), this penultimate stress is supported instrumentally by greater vowel duration and amplitude on the stressed syllable, and Gerfen treats laryngealization as licensed only under stress (on V1).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; stress is described as predictable ('falls predictably on the first vowel'). Penner 2019 (p. 92) notes that other Mixtec varieties show shifts or tone-stress interactions but lists Coatzospan among the plain penultimate-stress descriptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the couplet (the bimoraic root/morpheme, (C)CVV or (C)CVCV), i.e. the lexical word in citation form; the study measured words uttered in isolation. Nothing is said about longer words with affixes or clitics or about phrase-level prominence. The language is tonal (contrastive H/L tone patterns on couplets) with stress independent of tone.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Mixtec of San Juan Coatzospan (Sierra Mazateca, northern Oaxaca), i.e. coat1241 / ISO miz itself; Gerfen's fieldwork (1993-1997) was in that village. No other variety is involved. WALS code mxz 'Mixtec (Coatzospan)' is the same lect.

new_statements.quote: [p. 409] In ordinary vocative forms, stress and length fall on the first syllable of a couplet, just as they do in nonvocative forms, but the accent patterns sometimes differ. In vocative forms used when calling from a distance, the final syllable is stressed and lengthened and carries a high-low accent. [p. 268] There are three tone accents: high (written with acute accent), low (written with macron), and a rare high-low glide (written with circumflex). Unaccented syllables do not carry contrastive tone; they assimilate to the tone of the following syllable. [...] In nonnuclear positions, stems are unstressed and undergo various reductions.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement (Gerfen & Denisowski 1999: stress on the first vowel of a (C)CVCV couplet) and the catalog reading 'fixed: initial syllable': Small states stress and length fall on the first syllable of the couplet. Adds: length as a stress correlate, the 'tone accent' analysis (unaccented syllables toneless/assimilating), phrase-level destressing of nonnuclear stems, and the vocative exceptions with final stress. The catalog record itself (world-r2-2026-09-17) has an empty rule; this supplies a primary-source rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (with vowel length as its correlate) falls on the first syllable of the (bisyllabic) couplet, i.e. the root/stem, in ordinary forms. The language is tonal, described as three 'tone accents' (high, low, rare high-low glide) carried by accented syllables; unaccented syllables have no contrastive tone and take the tone of the following syllable. Stress is also phrase-sensitive: only the stem in the nucleus of the phonological phrase keeps its full (stressed) form; stems in pre- and post-nuclear position are unstressed and reduced. Fuller phonology deferred to Pike & Small 1974.
new_statements.exceptions: Vocatives: in 'calling' vocative forms the final syllable is stressed, lengthened and carries a high-low accent; in 'emphatic' vocatives VV/VhV reduce to V and stress shifts to the final syllable, which is checked by h (p. 409-410, with paradigms e.g. uva / uva / uvah 'Father!'). Stems in nonnuclear phrase positions are unstressed and reduced (prenuclear: loss of first member of geminate vowel, loss of glottal stop; postnuclear: reduced to one syllable), pp. 268-269. The grammar's 'prestressed'/'poststressed' pronoun, deictic and adverb classes (secs. 3.1, 5.4, 5.5) are these unstressed clitic-like forms. Aspect is marked by high/low 'accent' (tone) changes on the first syllable of the verb (sec. 5.1.2, pp. 398-400) -- tonal, not stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Small 1990 describes the variety of the municipal center San Juan Coatzospan, district of Teotitlan de Flores Magon, Oaxaca (sec. 0.1, p. 267: 'This study is based on the variety spoken in San Juan'); examples cited in men's speech; data 1963-1985 (Jose Pacheco Castro, Dolores Acosta de Campanela). Same variety as Gerfen's work (San Juan Coatzospan).
